title: What the Ontario Building Code asks of an ICF wall | GTA ICF
description: How Ontario's 2024 Building Code treats flat ICF walls: Part 9 limits, Subsections 9.15.4 and 9.20.17, concrete, drainage, footings, SB-12 and permits.
h1: What Ontario's Building Code asks of an ICF wall
lede: Ontario's 2024 Building Code carries prescriptive rules for flat insulating concrete form walls: Subsection 9.15.4 for foundation walls and Subsection 9.20.17 above ground, for houses up to 2 storeys with floor-to-floor heights up to 3 m. This guide is for homeowners, designers and builders who want to know what those rules ask for, where an engineer takes over, and what the building department checks on site. Every clause is cited from the ministry's digital Compendium, which is not the official Code, so confirm a clause against e-Laws before relying on it. We also say where a conventional or engineered wall is the better route.

sections.heading: Where Part 9 stops and an engineer starts
paragraphs: Part 9 covers housing and small buildings, and it treats a flat ICF wall as a prescriptive assembly as long as the building stays inside stated limits. Clause 9.15.1.1.(1)(c) applies Section 9.15 to flat ICF foundation walls and their footings on three conditions. The wall is not subject to surcharge. The soil is stable, with an allowable bearing pressure of 75 kPa or more. The building is of light-frame or flat ICF construction, not more than 2 storeys, with a floor-to-floor height of not more than 3 m. Clause 9.20.1.1.(1)(b) repeats the 3 m and 2 storey limits for ICF walls above ground and adds a seismic one: the site's Sa(0.2) must not be greater than 0.4.

Outside those limits the wall is designed to Part 4 by a professional engineer. Sentence 9.15.1.1.(2) sends other foundations to Section 9.4, Sentence 9.20.1.1.(2) sends other above-ground walls to Subsection 4.3.2, and Sentence 9.3.1.1.(3) sends reinforced concrete outside Subsection 9.15.4 to Part 4. Filled ground, peat or sensitive clay under the footing triggers Section 4.2 footing design on its own (9.15.1.1.(3)). In practice that means more than 2 storeys, a floor-to-floor height over 3 m, soil under 75 kPa, a surcharge from sloping ground or a load beside the wall, or a high-seismic site.

This is also where we say an ICF wall is not always the better choice. A wall over 3 m or soft ground under 75 kPa leaves the Part 9 tables and needs an engineer. A walk-out with wide openings, or a plan with many jogs, can stay inside Part 9 but pushes against its opening and support rules. There a poured and insulated wall, or a plan with fewer and narrower openings, is often simpler to review. We say which at the site review, not after the permit is in. Every clause here comes from the ministry's digital Compendium, which states it is not an official copy of the Code; confirm a clause on e-Laws before relying on it.

sections.heading: Foundation walls: Subsection 9.15.4
paragraphs: Article 9.15.4.1 asks every flat wall ICF unit to conform to CAN/ULC-S717.1, the material standard for the forms. Sentence 9.15.4.2.(2) sets the concrete core at not less than the greater of 150 mm (6 in) or the thickness of the concrete in the wall above. An 8 in wall above ground cannot sit on a 6 in foundation. Sentence 9.15.4.2.(1) then points to Table 9.15.4.2.-A, which gives the maximum height of finished ground above the basement floor for each core thickness and concrete strength, for walls up to 3.0 m in unsupported height. The rows for 150 and 200 mm cores are below; the table also carries 250 and 300 mm rows.

Sentence 9.15.4.2.(2.1) requires an ICF foundation wall to be laterally supported at top and bottom. The top counts when the wall carries an ICF or solid masonry wall above. It also counts when the floor joists are fixed to it under Article 9.20.17.5. That means a ledger at least 38 mm thick and as deep as the joists, on anchor bolts embedded at least 100 mm and spaced to Table 9.20.17.5. The bottom counts as supported in three cases (9.15.4.4). Backfill is 1.2 m or less. A shear key at the footing pairs with the floor framing. Or the wall is dowelled to the footing with 15M bars at 1.2 m or 10M bars at 600 mm on centre.

Reinforcing follows Article 9.15.4.5. Horizontal steel is one 10M bar within 300 mm of the top of the wall plus 10M bars at not more than 600 mm on centre. It sits in the inside half of the wall with 30 mm of cover from the inside face. Vertical steel comes from Tables 9.15.4.5.-A to -C by core thickness, ground height and wall height, also in the inside half. For example, a 150 mm wall with up to 1.35 m of ground above the basement floor takes 10M bars at 400 mm on centre. The spacing closes as the ground gets higher. The bar schedule on the drawings comes from those tables. The inspector checks it before the pour.
list: Under an opening wider than 1.2 m, or where openings take more than 25% of the wall length, the wall below counts as unsupported at the top unless reinforced for earth pressure (9.15.4.3.(3)).
Vertical bars interrupted by an opening sit within 600 mm of each side of it; reinforcing around the opening follows 9.20.17.3 or 9.20.17.4 (9.15.4.5.(2) and (4)).
A cold joint takes 15M bars at not more than 600 mm on centre, embedded at least 300 mm on both sides (9.15.4.5.(3)).
The foundation wall extends at least 150 mm above finished ground (9.15.4.6).

sections.heading: Walls above ground: Subsection 9.20.17
paragraphs: Above the foundation, Subsection 9.20.17 applies. Article 9.20.17.1 sets the concrete in a flat ICF wall not in contact with the ground at not less than 140 mm, constant for the entire height of the wall. The core cannot step down partway up a storey. Article 9.20.17.2 puts the steel in the middle third of the wall section. Horizontal steel is one 10M bar within 300 mm of the top plus 10M bars at not more than 600 mm on centre. Vertical steel is 10M bars at not more than 400 mm on centre. Bars interrupted by an opening are placed within 600 mm of each side of it. Most houses use a 6 in or 8 in core.

Openings are where the prescriptive path gets specific, and the rules differ for loadbearing and non-loadbearing walls. Both keep openings at least 1,200 mm from interior and exterior corners. In a loadbearing wall, Article 9.20.17.4 requires a lintel over every opening wider than 900 mm, built to Span Tables 9.20.17.4.-A, -B or -C. Lintels over openings wider than 1,200 mm also carry 10M stirrups for shear. Their spacing is not more than half the distance from the bottom bar to the top of the lintel. A wide walk-out door or a garage door on the loadbearing side of a plan is therefore a lintel design question before it is a form question.

Article 9.20.17.7 requires an above-ground ICF wall to be protected from precipitation and damage in conformance with Section 9.27, the cladding section. The EPS face is not a finish and is not left exposed: cladding, flashing and a drained cavity or drainage plane go on as they would over a framed wall, fastened to the form's web flanges. Below grade the same foam is protected by the dampproofing or waterproofing membrane and by careful backfilling, which the next sections cover. The Code says nothing about which ICF system to use; the form is whichever S717.1-conforming system the local supplier stocks, named on the quote.
list: Non-loadbearing walls keep at least 200 mm of concrete over every opening (9.20.17.3.(2)).
Non-loadbearing openings over 600 mm and up to 3,000 mm wide take one 10M bar top and bottom; over 3,000 mm, two 10M bars on all four sides, run 600 mm past the opening (9.20.17.3.(3) to (5)).
Openings in a non-loadbearing wall total no more than 70% of its length (9.20.17.3.(6)).
Floor ledgers are at least 38 mm thick and joist depth, on anchor bolts embedded 100 mm and spaced to Table 9.20.17.5: 12.7 mm bolts at 450 mm for a 2.44 m clear span, 275 mm at 5.00 m (9.20.17.5).
Roof framing bears on top plates anchored with bolts at least 12.7 mm in diameter at not more than 1,200 mm on centre, centred in the wall and embedded 100 mm (9.20.17.6).

sections.heading: Concrete, steel and the pour: Sentence 9.3.1.1.(4)
paragraphs: Sentence 9.3.1.1.(4) gives the materials rule for a flat ICF wall inside the Part 9 limits: the concrete and reinforcing either comply with Part 4 or meet two prescriptive conditions. The concrete conforms to CSA A23.1 with a maximum aggregate size of 19 mm, small enough to flow around the webs and bars inside the form. The reinforcing conforms to CSA G30.18, has a minimum specified yield strength of 400 MPa, and is lapped at least 450 mm for 10M bars and 650 mm for 15M bars. Those laps are what an inspector measures at the pre-pour visit, along with bar size, spacing and the position of the steel in the section.

Strength is chosen from Table 9.15.4.2.-A rather than fixed by one number. The table is written for 15 MPa and 20 MPa minimum strengths, and the higher strength buys backfill height for the same core. A 150 mm core supported at the top on a wall of 2.5 m or less goes from 1.5 m of finished ground to 1.8 m. A 200 mm core goes from 2.15 m to 2.3 m. The strength on the drawings is the strength on the delivery ticket, and the ready-mix supplier's mix design goes in the file with the pour record.

We pour year-round; in cold weather the concrete arrives warm, the wall is covered and the cure is allowed for, which adds time and can add cost. The rules behind that come from CSA A23.1. Any pour with a forecast below 5 °C in the next 24 hours is cold-weather work. Concrete for walls under 300 mm thick must arrive at 10 to 32 °C. It is kept at 10 °C or more through curing, and it reaches 7 MPa before it can see frost. The foam form helps hold that heat, but the open top of the wall and the footing still need cover, and snow and ice are cleared from the cavity before the pump arrives.

sections.heading: Dampproofing, drainage and footing depth
paragraphs: An ICF foundation is still a below-grade concrete wall, and Sections 9.13 and 9.14 treat it as one. Sentence 9.13.2.1.(1) requires the exterior surface of every foundation wall below ground level to be dampproofed, from finished ground down to the top of the footing (9.13.2.4), unless the wall is waterproofed instead. Where hydrostatic pressure occurs, Sentence 9.13.3.1.(1) makes waterproofing mandatory. Two sentences are written for ICF specifically: 9.13.2.3.(3) and 9.13.3.3.(2) say that when dampproofing or waterproofing goes onto an ICF wall, the ICF manufacturer's instructions are followed. Form makers publish those instructions and sell peel-and-stick membranes made for foam; the membrane on our quotes is matched to the system named there.

Drainage is Section 9.14. Sentence 9.14.2.1.(1) requires drainage at the bottom of every foundation wall that contains building interior, and Subsection 9.14.3 sets the weeping tile size and stone cover listed below. Sentence 9.14.2.1.(1.1) matters more for ICF than for a bare poured wall. Where the insulation on a foundation wall extends more than 900 mm below grade, as a full-height ICF basement wall does, a drainage layer is required against the outside of the wall. It runs down to the footing and sits on the outside face of the insulation. It is waived where the wall is waterproofed. Hamilton looks for the drainage layer, weeping tile and stone cover at its backfill inspection.

Depth comes from Table 9.12.2.2. With a heated basement, the minimum depth on clay or soils not clearly defined is 1.2 m, and there is no limit on rock or coarse-grained soils. Where there is no heated space, clay and undefined soils take 1.2 m but not less than the depth of frost penetration. Sentence (2) treats a foundation insulated so as to reduce heat flow to the soil under its footings as one with no heated space. Whether a full-height insulated wall does that is a point to settle with the reviewer, not to assume. Geotechnical reports filed with Hamilton and Burlington use 1.2 m as the design frost depth.
list: Weeping tile: not less than 100 mm in diameter, its top below the underside of the slab, under at least 150 mm of clean crushed stone (9.14.3.2 and 9.14.3.3).
Drainage layer options: at least 19 mm of mineral fibre insulation at 57 kg/m³ or more, at least 100 mm of free-draining granular material, or a system shown to perform the same (9.14.2.1.(1.1)).
Backfill goes in without damaging the wall, tile, drainage layer, insulation or membrane, and is graded to drain away from the wall (9.12.3.1 and 9.12.3.2).
Footings rest on undisturbed soil, rock or compacted granular fill (9.12.2.1 and 9.15.3.2).
Strip footings start at 250 mm wide for one supported floor, 350 mm for two and 450 mm for three, plus 150 mm for each storey of ICF wall the foundation carries (Table 9.15.3.4 and 9.15.3.5.(1)(c)).
A lesser footing depth is permitted where local experience with the soil, or a design, shows it is satisfactory (9.12.2.2.(5)).

sections.heading: SB-12 and the R10-each-face sentence
paragraphs: Energy efficiency for houses lives in Supplementary Standard SB-12, in Volume 2 of the Compendium. Zone 1 covers the GTA, Hamilton, Guelph and Niagara. There, compliance package A1 lists a minimum nominal RSI 3.52 continuous (about R-20) for basement walls and nominal RSI 3.87 (about R-22) for walls above grade. The effective values are RSI 3.72 and 3.00. ICF gets its own sentence. Sentence 3.1.1.2.(5) deems an ICF wall with at least RSI 1.76 (R10) of insulation on each face of the concrete to comply with the wall values in Table 3.1.1.2.A. Sentence (6) allows it in place of basement walls that need RSI 3.52 ci (R20) or less.

Three notes. The deemed-to-comply sentence is about the insulation on the faces of the concrete, so what matters at plan review is the EPS thickness of the chosen form and its manufacturer's tested thermal values, nominal separated from effective. Reviewers may ask for that product literature or third-party thermal test data with the SB-12 submission. A walk-out also has its own rule: Sentence 3.1.1.1.(10) asks the basement wall with the door, and any basement wall more than half exposed above ground, to meet the above-grade wall value. What the numbers mean for a real basement, and why we print no savings percentage, is covered in the R-value guide at /guides/r-value-thermal-savings-icf-basements/.

sections.heading: Permits and inspections in the GTA and Hamilton
paragraphs: Within the Part 9 limits an ICF wall can be drawn by a qualified designer. Beyond them, or when the reviewer asks, an engineer seals the wall design, and Toronto requires its Assumption of Responsibility for Engineering Content form. None of the six municipal websites publishes an ICF-specific checklist, so the package is the ordinary Part 9 one: plans, sections with footing and foundation wall details, the bar schedule, the SB-12 submission and product literature if the reviewer asks for it. Toronto asks sections to show the height of exterior grade above the basement floor, the number Table 9.15.4.2.-A turns on. We prepare the package with you; the documentation for the system named on the quote goes in it.

On site, Toronto, Hamilton, Mississauga and Oakville all inspect footing forms and rebar before concrete is placed and the foundation again before backfill. Mississauga's inspector also checks the bearing soil at the footing stage against the design value, 75 kPa for typical residential design, the same figure Part 9 hangs on, and that the reinforcement matches the permit drawings. Hamilton's backfill visit checks the drainage layer, weeping tile and stone cover. Oakville's pre-backfill inspection wants a site survey with the top-of-foundation elevation submitted first for new construction. Burlington's and Guelph's stage lists were not retrievable online when we checked, so confirm them with the building department.

With ICF the difference is what the inspector can see. The steel is checked through the open top and the cavity of a foam form, so the bar schedule, laps and cover must be visible before the pour. The membrane and drainage layer are inspected on foam rather than on concrete, and the backfill has to go in without gouging either. The municipal pages ask for nothing ICF-specific. The Code asks for a form that conforms to CAN/ULC-S717.1, not for a CCMC number. The NRC registry lists two ICF systems under S717.1 and one code-compliance report; other systems hold S717.1 listings from other accredited bodies. Where the system on your quote carries one, it goes in the package.

faqs.q: Does an ICF foundation in Ontario need an engineer?
faqs.a: Not always. Ontario's 2024 Building Code carries prescriptive rules for flat ICF walls in Subsections 9.15.4 and 9.20.17, for houses up to 2 storeys with floor-to-floor heights up to 3 m on stable soil of 75 kPa or more without surcharge. Inside those limits a qualified designer can draw the wall. Outside them, or when the reviewer asks, a professional engineer designs the wall to Part 4 and seals the drawings.

faqs.q: How much backfill can go against a 6 in ICF foundation wall?
faqs.a: Table 9.15.4.2.-A sets it by core, strength and support. A 150 mm (6 in) core at 15 MPa allows 0.8 m of finished ground above the basement floor when the wall is unsupported at the top. Supported at the top, on a wall of 2.5 m or less, it allows 1.5 m. At 20 MPa the supported figure rises to 1.8 m. A 200 mm (8 in) core allows 1.2 m unsupported and 2.15 m or 2.3 m supported. Confirm the values on e-Laws.

faqs.q: Do ICF basement walls still need waterproofing and weeping tile?
faqs.a: Yes. The Code requires the outside of every below-grade foundation wall to be dampproofed, or waterproofed where there is hydrostatic pressure, and drained at the footing. Because the insulation on an ICF wall runs more than 900 mm below grade, Sentence 9.14.2.1.(1.1) also requires a drainage layer against the wall unless it is waterproofed. The dampproofing and waterproofing articles say the ICF manufacturer's instructions are followed, and the form makers sell peel-and-stick membranes for foam.

faqs.q: How deep do footings go for an ICF basement in the GTA?
faqs.a: Table 9.12.2.2 sets a 1.2 m minimum footing depth for a heated basement on clay or soils not clearly defined, with no limit on rock or coarse-grained soils, and 9.12.2.1 requires excavations to reach undisturbed soil. Toronto and Hamilton publish no house footing depth of their own; geotechnical reports filed with Hamilton and Burlington use 1.2 m as the design frost depth. The Code allows less where local experience or a design shows it is satisfactory.

faqs.q: Does an ICF wall automatically meet SB-12 in Ontario?
faqs.a: SB-12 deems an ICF wall with at least RSI 1.76 (R10) of insulation on each face of the concrete to comply with the wall values in Table 3.1.1.2.A. It also allows that wall in place of basement walls that need RSI 3.52 ci (R20) or less. Whether a given form reaches R10 per face is read from its manufacturer's data sheet, and the submission names the form and its EPS thickness; reviewers may ask for product literature or third-party thermal test data. The R-value guide explains the difference.

faqs.q: Do I need a CCMC report to get a building permit for ICF?
faqs.a: The Code does not ask for one. Article 9.15.4.1 asks for a flat-wall form that conforms to CAN/ULC-S717.1. Some systems also carry a CCMC listing or evaluation report; the NRC registry shows two ICF systems under S717.1 and one code-compliance report, while other systems hold S717.1 listings from other accredited bodies. None of the six municipal websites we checked publishes an ICF-specific checklist, though a reviewer can still ask for product literature. The system is named on the quote and its documentation goes in the permit package.

cta.heading: Send us the drawings before the permit goes in
cta.body: Send the plans or a sketch with wall heights, the grade against each wall and any soil report. We will tell you whether the wall sits inside Part 9 or needs an engineer, prepare the permit package with you, and give a written quote after a site review.
